# Deformation Field Parametrization


## Overview
Deformation Field Parametrization addresses the problem of rendering dynamic, non-rigid scenes by mapping time-varying coordinates to a static canonical space, thereby decoupling geometry deformation from appearance [S1, unofficial]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Dynamic Scene Representation](13340-dynamic-scene-representation.md) by explicitly parameterizing the displacement field (e.g., via MLPs, splines, or hybrid models) rather than relying solely on explicit mesh tracking or full spatio-temporal neural networks, allowing for topology-preserving motion modeling with lower memory overhead [S1, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family rely on the shared principles of deformation field parametrization [12731-deformation-field-parametrization.md], where a query point $\mathbf{x}_t$ at time $t$ is transformed into a canonical coordinate $\mathbf{x}_c$ [12731-deformation-field-parametrization.md].

The core mechanism involves a deformation function $f_{\Delta}$ that predicts a displacement vector $\Delta$ based on the query point, time, and potentially auxiliary geometric or pose parameters. The canonical coordinate is computed as:

$$
\mathbf{x}_c = \mathbf{x}_t + \Delta(\mathbf{x}_t, \theta_t)
$$

where $\theta_t$ represents driving signals such as pose, expression coefficients, or time [S1, unofficial]. This canonical point $\mathbf{x}_c$ is then queried from a static radiance field $F_{\text{static}}$ to obtain density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$:

$$
(\sigma, \mathbf{c}) = F_{\text{static}}(\mathbf{x}_c)
$$

The final pixel color is computed using the standard emission-absorption model [44-radiance-field-optimization.md]:

$$
\hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i)) \mathbf{c}_i
$$

where $T_i = \exp\left(-\sum_{j=1}^{i-1} \sigma_j \delta_j\right)$ [44-radiance-field-optimization.md].

## Subtopics

### [Deformation-Guided Neural Fields](12044-deformation-guided-neural-fields.md)
Deformation-Guided Neural Fields extend static Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to dynamic scenes by introducing a deformation field that maps time-varying coordinates to a canonical space. Unlike static NeRF, which assumes a rigid scene, this method solves the problem of rendering articulated or deformable subjects (such as human faces) by decoupling geometry deformation from appearance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like [Neural Deformation Field](12724-neural-deformation-field.md) by explicitly guiding the deformation MLP with a parametric morphable 3D face model (3DMM), ensuring physically plausible facial topology and enabling explicit control over pose and expression parameters.

### [Neural Deformation Field](12724-neural-deformation-field.md)
The Neural Deformation Field (NDF) is a method for modeling non-rigid deformations in dynamic scenes by predicting a per-point displacement vector in canonical space, conditioned on pose and geometric attributes. It solves the problem of representing articulated or soft-tissue motion that Linear Blend Skinning (LBS) cannot capture due to its rigid-bone assumption. Unlike sibling methods that may bake geometry into static proxies, the NDF jointly optimizes the deformation network with the radiance field from scratch, allowing for direct geometry and texture editing.

### Spline-based Deformation Field
#### definition
- [S1, unofficial] A deformation field parametrization using cubic B-splines with time-modulated weights to map spatial coordinates $(x, y, z)$ at time $t$ to canonical coordinates $(x_0, y_0, z_0)$, enabling reconstruction from sparse projections.

#### step
- [S1, unofficial] Calculate the deformation field from sparse few-projection data recorded at intermediate times $t$ during the dynamic experiment.
- [S1, unofficial] Obtain full field spatio-temporal information by combining the canonical volume and the calculated deformation field.

#### pitfall
- [S1, unofficial] Deformation fields based on canonical models fail when the scene topology changes over time, as they assume topology-preserving motion.

#### comparison
- [S1, unofficial] Unlike methods using general MLP architectures for deformation fields which require complex regularization like elastic energy, this method uses cubic B-splines to enable reconstruction from as few as two projections.

### Local Rotation Estimation via SVD
#### definition
- [S2, unofficial] A technique to estimate the local rotation of each point during deformation to correct view-dependent rendering artifacts caused by large rotations.

#### step
- [S2, unofficial] Estimate location rotation for each point during deformation using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), borrowing the idea from ARAP.
- [S2, unofficial] Interpolate the estimated per-point rotation to the query view direction of the pre-trained radiance field.
- [S2, unofficial] Use the interpolated rotation to redirect the querying ray in the right direction, ensuring consistency between deformed and canonical space representations.

## Background
The concept of using canonical models with deformation fields was introduced to address the limitations of full spatio-temporal neural radiance fields, which can be ill-conditioned and require complex regularizers [S1, unofficial]. Early approaches parametrized temporal evolution using discrete timesteps with linear interpolation or continuous grid displacements obtained from MLPs [S1, unofficial]. The drawback of canonical models is their inability to handle topological changes, necessitating spatio-temporal networks or low-rank decomposition for such cases [S1, unofficial]. Recent developments include spline-based parametrizations for sparse data reconstruction [S1, unofficial] and local rotation estimation via SVD to handle large rotations in point-based radiance fields [S2, unofficial].
